english: the person themselves; the person in question
use: Points to the person being talked about, as opposed to others speaking for them.

example.romaji: honnin ni kiite yo.
example.ja: 本人に聞いてよ。
example.english: Just ask them directly.

examplePolite.ja: ご本人に聞いてください。

notes: Add go- (gohonnin) when speaking politely about someone else.

use: Also used casually for young women, not just children.

example.romaji: ano onna no ko, dare?
example.ja: あの女の子、誰？
example.english: Who's that girl?

examplePolite.romaji: ano onna no ko wa dare desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: あの女の子は誰ですか？

use: The everyday polite way to say kyaku; used by staff and hosts alike.

example.romaji: kyou wa okyakusan ooi ne.
example.ja: 今日はお客さん多いね。
example.english: Lots of customers today, huh.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa okyakusan ga ooi desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 今日はお客さんが多いですね。
examplePolite.english: There are a lot of customers today.

notes: Shop staff say okyakusama to customers' faces.

english: company president; head of a company
use: Also used like a name to address the president directly.

example.romaji: shachou mou kaetta?
example.ja: 社長もう帰った？
example.english: Has the boss gone home already?

examplePolite.ja: 社長はもう帰りましたか？
examplePolite.english: Has the president gone home already?

notes: Owners of small businesses are called shachou too.

use: The plain form; sounds blunt on its own, so say okyakusan when customers can hear.

example.romaji: ano mise, kyaku zenzen inakatta yo.
example.ja: あの店、客全然いなかったよ。
example.english: That place had no customers at all.

examplePolite.romaji: ano mise wa kyaku ga zenzen imasen deshita.
examplePolite.ja: あの店は客が全然いませんでした。
examplePolite.english: That shop had no customers at all.

use: The neutral, polite word used on forms, in shops and on the news; in chat people say otoko no hito.

example.romaji: dansei no hou ga ooi ne.
example.ja: 男性の方が多いね。
example.english: There are more men, huh.

examplePolite.romaji: dansei no hou ga ooi desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 男性の方が多いですね。
examplePolite.english: There are more men, aren't there?

use: Most often in X no mikata (on X's side).

example.romaji: watashi wa zutto mikata da kara ne.
example.ja: 私はずっと味方だからね。
example.english: I'll always be on your side.

examplePolite.romaji: watashi wa zutto mikata desu kara.
examplePolite.ja: 私はずっと味方ですから。
examplePolite.english: I'll always be on your side.

notes: Opposite: teki (enemy). Mix-up: mikata also means 'way of seeing' (見方).

example.romaji: kareshi iru no?
example.ja: 彼氏いるの？
example.english: Do you have a boyfriend?

notes: Girlfriend is kanojo. Use iru, not aru: kareshi ga iru.

use: Gender-neutral and a bit more serious than kareshi or kanojo.

example.romaji: koibito to issho ni sunderu n da.
example.ja: 恋人と一緒に住んでるんだ。
example.english: I live with my partner.

examplePolite.romaji: koibito to issho ni sunde imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 恋人と一緒に住んでいます。

use: The formal word for friend, used in introductions and speeches; in chat say tomodachi.

example.romaji: kochira wa daigaku jidai no yuujin desu.
example.ja: こちらは大学時代の友人です。
example.english: This is a friend from my university days.

use: Used casually for women of any age, and in school and sports for the girls' side.

example.romaji: kyou wa joshi dake de nomu n da.
example.ja: 今日は女子だけで飲むんだ。
example.english: Tonight it's just us girls drinking.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa joshi dake de nomimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は女子だけで飲みます。
examplePolite.english: Tonight it's just the women drinking.

notes: Pairs with danshi. joshikai = a girls' night out.

use: Anyone above you at work; said about them, not to them.

example.romaji: joushi ni mata okorareta.
example.ja: 上司にまた怒られた。
example.english: My boss yelled at me again.

examplePolite.ja: 上司にまた怒られました。
examplePolite.english: I got scolded by my boss again.

notes: Opposite: buka (subordinate). To their face, use their title or name plus san.

use: Also used casually for young men.

example.romaji: akachan, otoko no ko datta n da.
example.ja: 赤ちゃん、男の子だったんだ。
example.english: Oh, the baby was a boy!

examplePolite.romaji: akachan wa otoko no ko datta n desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 赤ちゃんは男の子だったんですね。
examplePolite.english: So the baby was a boy.

use: Often X no daihyou (representing X), and for national teams: nihon daihyou.

example.romaji: kurasu no daihyou de supiichi suru n da.
example.ja: クラスの代表でスピーチするんだ。
example.english: I'm giving a speech for our class.

examplePolite.romaji: kurasu no daihyou de supiichi o shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: クラスの代表でスピーチをします。
examplePolite.english: I'll give a speech on behalf of the class.

notes: Also a title for the head of a company or group.

use: Used for women; for men say ikemen.

example.romaji: ano hito, sugoi bijin da ne.
example.ja: あの人、すごい美人だね。
example.english: She's gorgeous.

examplePolite.romaji: ano hito wa totemo bijin desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: あの人はとても美人ですね。

notes: bijinsan is a softer, friendly form.

use: Mainly university students; school kids are usually seito.

example.romaji: mada gakusei na no?
example.ja: まだ学生なの？
example.english: You're still a student?

use: Used like a name to address them, and for the head of a school club.

example.romaji: buchou ga yonderu yo.
example.ja: 部長が呼んでるよ。
example.english: The manager wants you.

examplePolite.ja: 部長が呼んでいますよ。
examplePolite.english: The department head is asking for you.

notes: Sits above kachou and below shachou.

use: Casual; also works like an adjective: ikemen da ne.

example.romaji: kare, kekkou ikemen ja nai?
example.ja: 彼、結構イケメンじゃない？
example.english: Isn't he pretty good-looking?

examplePolite.romaji: kare wa kekkou ikemen desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 彼は結構イケメンですね。

notes: For women, say bijin or kawaii.

use: A company's own staff; seishain is a full-time regular employee.

example.romaji: ano hito, uchi no shain ja nai yo.
example.ja: あの人、うちの社員じゃないよ。
example.english: That guy doesn't work for us.

examplePolite.romaji: ano hito wa uchi no shain ja arimasen.
examplePolite.ja: あの人はうちの社員じゃありません。
examplePolite.english: That person isn't one of our employees.

notes: kaishain (office worker) is a common answer to 'what do you do?'

use: The everyday neutral word; dansei is more formal, otoko can sound blunt.

example.romaji: sakki, shiranai otoko no hito ga kita yo.
example.ja: さっき、知らない男の人が来たよ。
example.english: Some man I didn't know came by earlier.

examplePolite.romaji: sakki, shiranai otoko no hito ga kimashita.
examplePolite.ja: さっき、知らない男の人が来ました。
examplePolite.english: A man I didn't know came by earlier.
